  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/17934</id>
    <published>2026-05-08T14:44:22Z</published>
    <updated>2026-05-08T14:44:25Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/liqoria-the-mac-dock-player-that-should-ve-been-built-in"/>
    <title>Liqoria: The Mac Dock Player That Should've Been Built In</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Liqoria" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBK2FrQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--2935b3a4ff7c078061d240c553c68435f0fc607a/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-05-08%20at%2010.29.14.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Liqoria
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The promise:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; A universal music controller that lives in your Dock and unifies Apple Music, Spotify, browsers, and more with animated artwork, real waveforms, and native Apple design.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If Apple were the company that so many people pretend that it is, it would make a music controller lives in your Dock and plays not just Apple Music but also Spotify, Youtube and more with animated artwork, real waveforms, using real native Apple design. The reality though, is that Apple Music is a storefront, not a music player.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Thankfully, we now have &lt;a href="https://www.liqoria.com/"&gt;Liqoria,&lt;/a&gt; which quietly removes the whole category of app-switching annoyances that plague every other macOS music player. The Dock placement is better than notch-only players. The feature set makes it more than just a controller. The design is more native-feeling than 99% of indie apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Liqoria proves three myths wrong at once:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;that all miniplayers belong in the menu bar&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;that you need multiple apps for different services&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;that Apple will one day build a proper music widget.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Liqoria Actually Does&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Four player modes in one app:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Dock Player&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; -- Dynamic Island-style player docked to the macOS Dock, controls integrated directly where apps live&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Floating Player&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; -- Draggable desktop player with full controls&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Menu Bar Player&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; -- Compact menu bar integration&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Lock Screen Player&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; -- Full-screen controls with animated artwork&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Liqoria doesn't just pass commands to Apple Music and call it a day. It is a standalone music player with built-in search, queue management, and playback control. You can search Apple Music and Spotify directly, manage your Now Playing queue (including Apple Music), and control playback without ever touching the source app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The multi-player view is the real weapon.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; See all active music sources at once -- Apple Music, Spotify, browser playback, anything exposing to Control Center -- and switch between them. Most competitors show one source or force you to cycle. Liqoria shows everything at a glance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The visual polish is borderline aggressive.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Real FFT waveform visualization (that pulsing audio graph from Dynamic Island), animated album art for supported tracks (SZA's "Kill Bill" actually animates on lock screen), and that liquid glass aesthetic stolen shamelessly from Apple's design language. It's the kind of UI that makes you check if it's using private frameworks (it is, which is why it's not on the App Store).&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Features Set&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Built-in search across platforms:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Search Apple Music and Spotify directly within Liqoria. No context-switching to the Music app or Spotify client. YouTube search is coming -- dev confirmed it's in progress but won't drop until it's ready.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Apple Music queue management:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Finally, see and manage your Now Playing queue from a miniplayer. Apple Music's own app doesn't even show this in mini mode. You can reorder, remove, and see what's coming next without opening the full app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Playback control that goes beyond play/pause:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Like, shuffle, repeat, scrubbing, and the waveform visualization gives you a visual read on track activity. The dock player responds to hover and integrates clean with the Dock's native behavior.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multi-source control:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; If you switch from YouTube Music to Apple Music, Liqoria can track the active source. The dev admits Apple's API makes this difficult -- play/pause sometimes grabs the wrong source -- but a dedicated YouTube controller mode is in progress to fix this.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Lyrics support:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Already displays lyrics with major updates incoming. Current implementation works; future version will be a significant overhaul.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Customization:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Switch between liquid glass and standard styles&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Configure dock player position (center/left/right)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Priority settings for multiple audio sources&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Keyboard shortcuts for everything&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Competition&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Silicio, VinylPod, Sleeve:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;These are solid but fundamentally limited. Most support only Apple Music and Spotify, lack built-in search, can't display multiple players simultaneously, and ship with the same queue control gap that Liqoria fills. Sleeve's album art integration is pretty, but it doesn't let you search Spotify or manage Apple Music queues without reaching for the source app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Dynamic Island clones (Menu Bar/Notch):&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;The notch obsession is the wrong approach. When the Island expands, it blocks menu bar items and reduces usable screen space on the MacBook. The Dock makes more sense for high-frequency controls -- your cursor's already there for app interaction. You can glance at playback without breaking focus on your main window.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Browser-based miniplayers:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Fine for one service, but they don't unify across sources. Liqoria's the unifier -- one player for everything, no matter where the audio comes from.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Real-World Use&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The workflow that clicks:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;You're working in a fullscreen app, music playing from Apple Music. A track comes up you want to pull up in Spotify to check the original or explore the artist. Instead of:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Cmd+Tab to Music&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Copy/paste search&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Jump to Spotify&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Search again&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You invoke Liqoria's search, switch sources, and never leave your workspace. The 72-hour trial is more than enough to decide if this friction removal is worth $9.90.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The dock player specifically:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;I run hidden docks (vertical on the left for screen real estate), so I was skeptical. But the dock player only appears when the dock is visible, and vertical dock support is coming in the next update ETA May-June. Even without that, the floating and menu bar modes cover the hidden dock use case.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The Apple Music queue fix:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/i-replaced-apple-music-with-yate-swinsian-navidrome-and-an-ipod-classic-surprisingly-better"&gt;I recently switched back to using my own curated music collection over subscription sources.&lt;/a&gt; If you rip CDs or build libraries instead of streaming, the queue view alone justifies the app. Apple Music's mini player shows track info and controls, but you can't see what's queued or reorder. Liqoria surfaces this without forcing you into the full Music app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What's Missing (Or Coming)&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Vertical dock support:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Confirmed for May-June timeframe. Current version works with horizontal docks and respects hidden dock behavior.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;YouTube search:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; In development, no ETA. Dev refuses to drop a half-baked implementation, which is the right call.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Lyrics overhaul:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; On the roadmap. Current support works but the dev promised "major improvements."&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Local file playback:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Not yet supported, but planned. Liqoria can control audio from Finder Quick Look and 99% of apps already, but direct local file playback is coming.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Scrobbling support:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Planned (&lt;a href="http://last.fm/"&gt;Last.fm&lt;/a&gt;, etc.), not yet implemented.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Minor bugs:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Some users report the menu panel not opening over fullscreen apps (opens to desktop instead). Dev is responsive -- moved conversation to Discord/email to debug directly. This is active development, not abandonware.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The App Store Question&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Why no App Store? The dev uses Apple private frameworks for browser music handling and Bluetooth device control. App Store review would reject this immediately. Direct download via Lemon Squeezy, 14-day refund window, lifetime license for up to 3 devices.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reality is you trade sandboxed convenience for the kind of deep system integration that makes Liqoria work. If you live inside the App Store walled garden, this isn't for you. If you want your music player to actually control your system, it's the only option.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Pricing &amp;amp; Availability&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;$9.90 lifetime license&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (up to 3 devices, deactivatable anytime). Free 72-hour trial -- full feature access, no credit card required. macOS 15.4+ required. Available at &lt;a href="http://liqoria.com/"&gt;liqoria.com&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is aggressively priced compared to competitors selling subscription models or charging $20+ for similar feature sets. The lifetime model alone puts it ahead of Sleeve and company.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Verdict&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;If you use multiple music services or want actual queue control, Liqoria is an instant buy.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;The multi-player view, built-in search, and Apple Music queue management quietly remove a whole category of friction that nobody else addresses.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;If you're happy with one service and don't care about queues&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, this might be overkill. A simpler miniplayer or the native controls will suffice.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;If you have a hidden dock&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, wait for the May-June update for full vertical dock support. The floating and menu bar modes work now, but you're not getting the headline feature without horizontal dock access.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The Dock vs. Notch debate is settled:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; The Dock makes more sense for high-frequency interaction. You're already glancing at it for other apps, and it doesn't block menu bar icons or eat screen space. The notch obsession is cool until you try to click that menu bar item and realize the Island ate your workspace.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Real Utility Defined:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Not in copying Dynamic Island visual flair, but in unifying disjointed audio sources in one place. Liqoria doesn't look native -- it is native, enough that some users on r/macapps genuinely thought it shipped with the OS.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;72-hour trial. If you switch between Apple Music, Spotify, and browser playback daily, you'll know whether this is worth $9 within an hour. The animations and waveforms are marketing; the unified control is why you keep it.&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/17909</id>
    <published>2026-05-06T19:21:42Z</published>
    <updated>2026-05-07T01:22:02Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/corel-painter-is-still-alive-and-still-ridiculously-good"/>
    <title>    Corel Painter Is Still Alive and Still Ridiculously Good</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Corel Painter" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBMStrQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d0695c8c130931bee2043d563b71570faaa91223/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-05-06%20at%2015.17.46.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Corel Painter
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Corel’s Spot on Memory Lane&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I hadn’t thought about &lt;a href="https://www.painterartist.com/en/"&gt;Corel graphics apps&lt;/a&gt; in a long time until I saw &lt;a href="https://bundlehunt.com/?ap_id=MacPicks"&gt;their flagship app on sale recently&lt;/a&gt;. I got my first tech-related job in 1994, when my ability to figure things out in Windows 3.1 earned me a promotion from the manufacturing floor to the quality department at the Westinghouse factory where I worked after getting out of the Army.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The tools I worked with felt absurdly expensive at the time: a Pentium PC, a Kodak digital camera, and the first color laser printer I’d ever seen. And then there was Corel; a professional suite of graphics tools I used to produce hundreds of technical work instructions for the people on the shop floor.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Corel still occupies a narrow but devoted niche in the graphics world. It’s loved by a small community of artists and designers and mostly ignored by everyone else in favor of mass-market tools from Adobe, Affinity, and a handful of others. The current version is Painter 2023. I took it for a spin and it’s more capable than anything else I’ve seen in its niche, but the real question is whether those capabilities matter to you.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;But What Is It?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Painter isn’t a drawing app or an image editor in the conventional sense. It’s a digital canvas simulator built for artists who want the feel of oil paint, watercolor, ink, and charcoal without the mess. The brush engine is the entire product. Everything else exists to support it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The target user is a professional illustrator, concept artist, or fine artist working with a Wacom or another pressure-sensitive tablet. If that’s not you, Painter probably isn’t for you, and Corel doesn’t pretend otherwise.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Brush Engine&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reality is that no software on any platform simulates natural media the way Painter does. Photoshop’s brushes are powerful but fundamentally digital. Procreate feels great on an iPad but remains a raster drawing tool. Clip Studio Paint has excellent line tools but doesn’t attempt to simulate paint physics at this level.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Painter 2023 ships with hundreds of brushes organized across dozens of categories: Oils, Acrylics, Watercolor, Gouache, Pastels, Chalk, Charcoal, Inks, and more. Each category behaves differently at the physics level. Watercolor bleeds and beads. Thick paint builds up and catches light. Impasto brushes create actual texture relief on the virtual canvas.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fluid Brushes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; iappear to be a real game changer. They’re built around layer transparency and allow subtle glazing and blending effects that previously required awkward workarounds. Corel claims they run up to 50 times faster by leveraging both CPU and GPU acceleration. On Apple Silicon hardware (my M4 Mac Mini), the effect is genuinely impressive.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Feature Set&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;900+ brushes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; covering nearly every traditional medium&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fluid Paint&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; with build, sculpt, and blend brushes plus precision opacity control&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Thick Paint&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; with three-dimensional impasto simulation&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Particle Brushes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; that flow, fork, and react dynamically&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Color Selection Brushes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; that combine selection and painting workflows&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;AI Photo Painting&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; tools powered by Core ML&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Clone Painting&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; for painting directly from reference photos&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Photoshop compatibility&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; with layered PSD read/write support&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Tablet support&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; for Wacom, Xencelabs, and Huion devices with pressure, tilt, rotation, and bearing support&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Customizable workspace&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; with movable palettes, panels, and brush libraries&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Catch&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is not an easy app to learn, even for experienced users. Nobody is going to master Painter in an afternoon. Corel provides tutorials, webinars, and learning materials through its Painter portal, and if you decide to invest time in the app, you’ll probably need them.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The UI looks exactly like what it is: decades of accumulated decisions packed into a single workspace. Tool panels feel cramped even on a large laptop display. Honestly, two monitors feels less like a luxury and more like a requirement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The current version is still Painter 2023. It runs fine on the last several macOS releases, including Apple Silicon Macs, but there was no 2024 or 2025 release, and it’s unclear whether there will be a 2026 version. I understand that it’s a mature product serving a mature niche, but some transparency about the development cycle would help inspire confidence.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Under normal circumstances, I couldn’t recommend that an individual pay the full perpetual-license price of $429. That’s the kind of software purchase employers are supposed to absorb. Especially when Procreate costs $12.99 and Clip Studio Paint EX runs about $50 a year.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But don’t stop reading yet.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Justification&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Right now, you can get a perpetual license for the full version of Painter 2023 for $49 from &lt;a href="https://bundlehunt.com/?ap_id=MacPicks"&gt; BundleHunt.&lt;/a&gt; That’s still real money, but it changes the equation dramatically.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you’re genuinely curious, already own a pressure-sensitive tablet, and have the artistic skills to take advantage of what Painter offers, this becomes much easier to justify. At that price, it’s less a reckless software purchase and more an opportunity to experiment with what is probably the most sophisticated paint-physics engine ever shipped on a desktop computer.&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/17898</id>
    <published>2026-05-05T18:32:33Z</published>
    <updated>2026-05-05T18:32:35Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/substage-a-natural-language-command-line-tool-for-finder"/>
    <title>Substage - A Natural Language Command Line Tool for Finder</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--png"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Substage" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBek9rQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--e75a2ceab9f04d19da20b63c13b5ad1fddd4f623/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--768aeab7fb7843d85fe5b2b4ba237e06e6ef604f/image.png" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Substage
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://selkie.design/substage/"&gt;Substage&lt;/a&gt; is a command bar that attaches beneath your Finder window. Select files, type what you want in plain English, and Substage generates a Terminal command, previews its side effects, and runs it with confirmation when needed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Think of it less as an AI assistant and more as a natural language layer between your intent and the Unix tools already built into macOS.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The key distinction; the AI’s role ends once the command is generated. After that, real shell tools do the work: &lt;code&gt;sips&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;ffmpeg&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;zip&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;qpdf&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;pandoc&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;git&lt;/code&gt;. No hallucinated output. No “trying until something works.” The command either works or it doesn’t, just like it would in Terminal.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Developer:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; Selkie Design — Joe Humfrey (u/joethephish)&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Platform:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; macOS 15.0 or later&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pricing:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; BYOK — $39.99. &lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/i-got-a-sneak-peek-at-the-spring-sale-at-bundlehunt"&gt;Currently on sale for $5 at Bundlehunt&lt;/a&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Website:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://selkie.design/substage/"&gt;substage.app&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Let’s Get One Thing Straight&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Even if you’re comfortable in the Terminal, it can still be tedious.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Using natural language to drive command-line tools isn’t about avoiding the shell; it’s about removing friction. I reach for Substage in the same situations where I’d otherwise open a converter app, type out a &lt;code&gt;sips&lt;/code&gt; command, or navigate into a deeply nested folder just to run something quick.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The goal isn’t to replace knowledge; it’s to make it easier to apply.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Features That Matter&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Substage Predicts&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;This is what makes the app practical.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Before running anything, Substage simulates the command using a custom interpreter that understands pipes, redirection, and arguments across a wide range of tools. You can see exactly what will happen; which files will be created, renamed, moved, or deleted.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This feeds into Auto-run:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Read-only operations can run automatically&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Destructive actions always require confirmation&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s not just a safety layer; it gives you confidence to use it for real work.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Instant Actions&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;For simple tasks, Substage skips the AI layer entirely. Commands like &lt;code&gt;jpg&lt;/code&gt;, &lt;code&gt;zip&lt;/code&gt;, or &lt;code&gt;mp4&lt;/code&gt; execute locally with no delay.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That keeps common operations fast and predictable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Command History&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Up-arrow cycles through previous commands, just like in Terminal. Small detail, but it makes repeat tasks and batch workflows much more practical.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Model Flexibility&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;By default, Substage uses GPT-4.1 Mini; fast and reliable for most tasks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The BYOK license lets you use your own API keys or local models via Ollama or LM Studio. OpenRouter and Perplexity also work with custom configuration.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Global Shortcut&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Ctrl-Space by default. Opens Substage under the active Finder window. Fast enough to become muscle memory.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Real-World Use Cases&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where it starts to earn its keep:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Batch image resizing across folders&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Video conversion with control over resolution, FPS, and bitrate&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;PDF workflows: merge, split, rotate, password protect, extract text&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Document conversion via &lt;code&gt;pandoc&lt;/code&gt; (DOCX ⇄ Markdown ⇄ HTML ⇄ EPUB)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;File metadata inspection - “Where did I download this?”&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Git operations without leaving Finder&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Quick system queries without opening System Information&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Numeric calculations using &lt;code&gt;bc&lt;/code&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It cuts out the need for one-off GUI wrappers around tools you already have.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Honest Limitations&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developer is clear about where things break down.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multi-step prompts are unreliable&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Chaining actions like “convert, rename, and zip into subfolders” can work, but reliability drops quickly. Better to split tasks into discrete steps.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Finder only&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;No support for Path Finder or ForkLift. If you don’t use stock Finder, this won’t fit your workflow.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Default Folder X conflicts&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Documented in the FAQ. If you rely on it, test carefully.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;No multimodal features&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;No image analysis, no transcription, no generative features. This is strictly a file operations tool.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Occasional lag&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;It can trail Finder updates slightly. Not constant, but noticeable.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Verdict&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Substage addresses a real gap; what macOS can do versus what you can remember how to ask it to do.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Natural language handles syntax&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;The simulator handles safety&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Native tools handle execution&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It won’t replace Hazel, and it’s not meant to.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What it replaces is the friction between intent and execution; opening another app, digging through menus, or reconstructing a command you last used months ago.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Caveats matter:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Default Folder X users should evaluate carefully&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Multi-step commands are hit or miss&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Finder dependency is real&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But within its lane; single-step, file-focused operations; it’s genuinely useful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you spend a lot of time in Finder and regularly convert, inspect, compress, or manipulate files, Substage removes a surprising amount of friction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;br&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Substage%20-%20A%20Natural%20Language%20Command%20Line%20Tool%20for%20Finder" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Substage is a command bar that attaches beneath your Finder window. Select files, type what you want in plain English, and Substage generates a Terminal command, previews its side effects, and runs it with confirmation when needed.

Think of it less as an AI assistant and more as a natural...</summary>

    <title>Find any File for $2: New BundleHunt Sneak Peek</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpeg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Find Any File" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBN0tqQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--665566c5295cae926f9b602d3265190348b26f67/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0FBaHBBZ0FHT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2dwemRISnBjRlE2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwWkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--fa3dbe24e376882dfd8c9dddfec0441143a8bd41/95154.jpeg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Find Any File
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The spring sale for &lt;a href="https://bundlehunt.com/?ap_id=MacPicks"&gt;Bundle Hunt&lt;/a&gt; doesn't officially open until tomorrow, but I have some inside info on what's coming this time around for the bargain hunters out there. One of my favorite apps for over two decades is going on sale for $2.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Mac users have a wide range of file search tools, from the built-in Spotlight to professional options like Foxtrot that cost north of $100. The right choice depends on how you actually search.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I tend to run the same kinds of queries repeatedly, so saved searches and reusable templates matter. I also frequently need to locate a specific file quickly, which means I care about a clean interface and fast launch.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;My go-to for day-to-day work is &lt;a href="https://bundlehunt.com/?ap_id=MacPicks"&gt;Find Any File (FAF)&lt;/a&gt;. It’s currently on sale at BundleHunt for $2, which is almost absurd given what it does. More importantly, it finds files that Spotlight simply won’t.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Spotlight is fast. It’s convenient. It’s also quietly omitting large parts of your filesystem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;FAF searches everywhere Spotlight skips: system and Library folders, hidden files, package contents, network volumes, and external disks. Most tools avoid these areas. FAF doesn’t.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Hold ⌥ in the search window and the &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Find&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; button changes to &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Find All&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Enter your admin password, and FAF relaunches with elevated privileges, allowing it to search other users’ home directories on the same Mac. That sounds niche until you actually need it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Spotlight only indexes what Apple chooses to include. System folders, many Library paths, network volumes, other users’ home directories, and files buried inside app bundles are often excluded. If you’ve ever tried to track down a preference file, cache, or config in &lt;code&gt;/Library&lt;/code&gt;, you’ve probably hit this wall: no results, no explanation, and no confidence the file is even there.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What It Is&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Find Any File, developed by Thomas Templeton, has been around for over two decades. The current version is 2.6.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Its core approach is straightforward: it searches the filesystem directly via BSD APIs instead of relying on Spotlight’s index. No index means no blind spots. If the file exists and your permissions allow it, FAF will find it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This isn’t a full replacement for Spotlight. It’s the tool you reach for when Spotlight comes up empty.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Key Features That Actually Matter&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Precise search rules&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;The search builder supports stacked criteria: filename (including wildcards and regex), extension, size, date ranges, file type, visibility, Trash status, and even Finder comments.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Real-world example: in a large &lt;code&gt;~/Music&lt;/code&gt; library, you can find every file that &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;isn’t&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; MP3 or AAC and is larger than 1 MB. That’s a simple three-condition query here; Spotlight can’t express it cleanly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Content search&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;FAF can search inside plain text files and compressed archives, including &lt;code&gt;.docx&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;.xlsx&lt;/code&gt;. With optional Spotlight integration enabled, you can also pull in PDF content results alongside FAF’s direct matches.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Hierarchical results view&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Flat lists break down quickly with large result sets. Switch to tree view (⌘2) and results are grouped by folder hierarchy, which makes triage and cleanup work much faster.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Saved searches&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Save any query as a &lt;code&gt;.faf&lt;/code&gt; file and rerun it with a double-click. This is where FAF becomes a workflow tool, not just a utility.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Example use case: auditing an Obsidian vault for non-markdown files (anything that isn’t &lt;code&gt;.md&lt;/code&gt;, an image, or a PDF).&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Automation hooks&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;FAF exposes a URL scheme and integrates cleanly with tools like Keyboard Maestro, PopClip, Default Folder X, and BBEdit. If your workflow is hotkey-driven, this is where it starts to compound.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;A Little Reality&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;FAF isn’t instant. It performs a live filesystem scan rather than querying an index.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On a fast SSD with a narrow scope, it’s quick enough. On a large spinning disk or wide search scope, it takes longer. That’s the tradeoff: completeness vs. speed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For the situations where you reach for FAF, completeness usually wins.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The UI is functional and very macOS-native. It uses the same criteria-building pattern as Finder searches and Smart Mailboxes, so there’s almost no learning curve if you’ve used those.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Pricing &amp;amp; Availability&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can grab it via BundleHunt during sales, or buy it outright on the Mac App Store as a one-time purchase. There’s also a direct download from the developer that runs as shareware: try it, pay if you keep using it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you already purchased the App Store version, you can run the direct version on the same Mac without buying it again. That’s a small detail, but it says a lot about the developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who It’s For&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Anyone who has run into Spotlight’s invisible boundaries:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;developers tracking down config files&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;power users auditing disk contents&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;admins who need full visibility&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;anyone who’s ever thought: &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;“this file exists, why can’t I find it?”&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;FAF isn’t flashy. It’s a precision tool for when Spotlight stops being honest about what’s on your disk.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Find%20any%20File%20for%20$2:%20New%20BundleHunt%20Sneak%20Peek" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

The spring sale for Bundle Hunt doesn't officially open until tomorrow, but I have some inside info on what's coming this time around for the bargain hunters out there. One of my favorite apps for over two decades is going on sale for $2.

Mac users have a wide...</summary>

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/17818</id>
    <published>2026-04-29T01:29:37Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-29T01:29:38Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/tolaria-a-files-first-markdown-app-for-mac-designed-for-git-workflows-and-ai-agents"/>
    <title>Tolaria: a files-first Markdown app for Mac designed for Git workflows and AI agents</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--png"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Tolaria" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBeUtpQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--2110fe116496acd97df7bf106cc5b4fc909dad62/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJY0c1bkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--768aeab7fb7843d85fe5b2b4ba237e06e6ef604f/tolaria-full-layout.png" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Tolaria
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://tolaria.md"&gt;Tolaria&lt;/a&gt; is a free, open-source desktop app for macOS and Linux built by Luca Rossi, the author of the &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;Refactoring&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; newsletter. Rossi created Tolaria to manage his own collection of 10,000+ notes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That origin story matters. The feature set feels like it grew out of solving real problems for a real workflow; not something assembled by a product manager or stitched together from an AI roadmap.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;At its core, Tolaria is a very 2026-style Markdown editor; modern, opinionated, and not trying to clone Notion or compete head-on with Obsidian.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The sweet-spot user is someone who:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Already lives in Markdown and Git&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Is experimenting with tools like Claude Code or other AI agents in their daily workflow&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Wants their knowledge base to be part of their AI context instead of isolated from it&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Treats data portability as a non-negotiable requirement&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Tolaria’s Core Principles&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These are deliberate design choices from the developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Files-first.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Notes are plain &lt;code&gt;.md&lt;/code&gt; files on disk. No proprietary database; no export step. Open them in BBEdit, Obsidian, Vim, or anything else that understands Markdown.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Git-first.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;Every vault is a Git repository. You get full version history and can push to any remote you like. There are no Tolaria servers; the app doesn’t depend on one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That alone sets it apart from a lot of the field.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Offline-first, zero lock-in.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;No account. No subscription. The vault works completely offline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Open source (AGPL-3.0).&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;The code lives on GitHub. You can read it, fork it, and run your own build if you want.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What It’s Not&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria is not trying to be Notion.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There’s no relational database layer, no property-driven schemas, and no team collaboration platform. That trade-off is intentional; those features usually come with heavier infrastructure and less portability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It also doesn’t have anything close to Obsidian’s plugin ecosystem. If your workflow depends on dozens of community plugins, Tolaria probably isn’t ready to replace Obsidian yet. It’s a younger, more focused tool.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Another practical detail: it runs on Mac and Linux only; there’s no Windows version. For some people that’s a dealbreaker. For others, it’s perfectly fine.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;AI Support and Integration&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where Tolaria earns its “second brain for the AI era” tagline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead of bolting on a chat sidebar, the app treats your knowledge vault as something AI agents can actually work with.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria includes built-in support for tools like Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI. It automatically generates a shared &lt;code&gt;AGENTS.md&lt;/code&gt; file in the vault root. That file explains the structure and conventions of your notes, and every supported AI tool reads the same one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The practical benefit: you maintain a single source of truth for how your vault is organized instead of writing separate instructions for each model you’re experimenting with.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria also runs a local MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. When you connect an external AI tool, your vault is registered as a structured context source that the agent can query directly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most “AI-enabled” note apps just add a chat window. Tolaria takes a different approach: it lets AI agents navigate and operate on the vault itself using standard protocols.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are also vault-level permission modes, so agents don’t automatically get full write access to your notes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Power-User Bonus Feature&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria clearly targets people who prefer keyboards over mice.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Command Palette is central to the workflow, and the editor is designed around keyboard navigation. If you spend time in tools like Raycast, Keyboard Maestro, or VS Code, the design philosophy will feel familiar.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is the difference between a command palette that drives the interface and one that feels bolted on as an afterthought.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Availability and Pricing&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tolaria is free and open source.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can download it from &lt;a href="https://tolaria.md"&gt;tolaria.md&lt;/a&gt; or build it yourself from the GitHub repository.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No subscription. No account. No catch.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Hat tip to &lt;a href="https://labnotes.org/weekend-reading-dream-of-bigger-things/?ref=labnotes-by-assaf-arkin-newsletter"&gt;Labnotes&lt;/a&gt; for once again, being the first to write about a new tool&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Tolaria:%20a%20files-first%20Markdown%20app%20for%20Mac%20designed%20for%20Git%20workflows%20and%20AI%20agents" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Tolaria is a free, open-source desktop app for macOS and Linux built by Luca Rossi, the author of the Refactoring newsletter. Rossi created Tolaria to manage his own collection of 10,000+ notes.

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/16235</id>
    <published>2026-04-21T17:06:17Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-21T17:06:19Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/dockside-turns-drag-and-drop-into-a-real-workflow"/>
    <title>Dockside Turns Drag-And-Drop Into a Real Workflow</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Dockside" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBenlUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c477ea28ee5cd6418e099737d9ba46f38cb5c80c/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-21%20at%2013.04.19.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Dockside
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most Mac users already rely on drag-and-drop constantly, but macOS never really gave us a good place to &lt;i&gt;&lt;em&gt;stage&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/i&gt; things temporarily. Finder windows work, but they’re clumsy for quick hand-offs between apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside turns that gap into a system. It acts like a permanent drop zone beside your Dock where you can park files, preview them, batch them, trigger actions, and move them between apps without juggling Finder windows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Turning Drag and Drop Into a System&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Just because you want to use a file shelf utility doesn’t mean you should have to manage yet another window cluttering your workspace.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Shelf location is a feature; an important one. With Dockside, the shelf lives beside your Dock or on any edge of your display you choose. It’s always where your muscle memory expects it. It’s definitely not another window you have to manage.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside’s strength isn’t just acting as a landing strip for files. It includes multiple purpose-built shelf areas, a secondary space for screenshots, downloads, recents, and clipboard history, plus stacks, Quick Look, utilities, and; this is where the real power lives; drop zones that can trigger Shortcuts, scripts, or file actions based on what you drop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What Dockside Is and Isn’t&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside is a native-feeling macOS file shelf and Dock companion. You drag in files, folders, apps, images, video, links, or text; park them temporarily; preview or batch-select them; then drag them out to Finder or into apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;not&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; a “Dock replacement.” It’s more like a workflow lane; close enough to the Dock to feel like it belongs to the OS, but customizable enough to act like a small command center.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Multi-Shelf Layout&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside gives each side of your Dock a different purpose.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Files shelf&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;The primary area where you drag files, folders, apps, images, video, links, or text.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Secondary shelf&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;br&gt;By default this displays screenshots and downloads, but it can be configured to show several other categories:&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Recent files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (with exclusions and limits)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Clipboard history&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (with capture toggles, exclusions, and regex rules)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Media controls&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (Spotify or Apple Music)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;System info&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; (CPU, memory, disk, network, battery, uptime, temperatures)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Dragging; Opinionated in a Good Way&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dragging items out of Dockside is sophisticated in a way that shows how much thought went into its design.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Smart drag activation:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; open when dragging starts, when the cursor nears the shelf, or when it approaches the cursor; user choice.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Adjustable sensitivity:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; tune the delay and drop-zone height so it feels fast without triggering accidentally.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Store by alias or copy:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; keep lightweight aliases or store real copies inside Dockside.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;
&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Remove items after drag-out:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; great for true hand-off workflows.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The attention to detail is clear in the modifier-key behavior while dragging. You can remove items on drag-out with &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Option&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, use Finder-style move vs copy behavior, ignore activation with &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fn&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, and more.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s the kind of app that gets noticeably better once your muscle memory kicks in.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;So Many Features&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’ve been using Dockside for over a year. During that time the feature set has grown quite a bit without drifting into feature bloat.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Project Scratchpad&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can create and manage up to three separately configurable work zones in Dockside (for example: working copies, archive, future projects), each with its own automation rules based on tag filters or watched folders.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Clutter isn’t much of a problem because Dockside includes a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;stack interface&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; and lets you create folders directly from selected files.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Drop Zones&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can configure multiple drop zones that appear when you drag items. Each zone has a user-definable primary action (Shortcut, Email, Copy or Move, AppleScript, shell script, CLI command, utilities, or none) and a post-drop action (keep in shelf, move or copy elsewhere, trash, or permanently delete).&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Utility Suite&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside includes a set of file utilities available from menus, hover actions, or assignable drop zones:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Compression and extraction&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Image to PDF&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Image metadata removal&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Rename&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Move or copy to predefined folders&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;ShareSheet&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Cloud uploads&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Clop integration for file size optimization&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Finder integration via a Finder Sync extension&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What Makes Dockside Stand Out&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The problem with many apps in this category is inconsistent behavior. Elements move around unexpectedly, or panels hide and unhide randomly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside has been rock solid in my experience.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can configure which display it appears on and which edge it attaches to. You choose how it hides or shows itself, either through settings or a global shortcut. Once configured, it behaves predictably. It just works.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It’s 100% a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Mac-ass Mac app&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Standard keyboard shortcuts work as expected: ⌘C, ⌘V, ⌘A, ⌘⌫, and ⌘Z to restore. Multi-item selection is built in. There are trackpad and mouse gestures for expanding shelves and paginating items. The right-click context menu is practical and thoughtfully designed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside is also Terminal friendly. It supports Apple Shortcuts and custom URLs. Not only does it work with Clop, it also includes a PopClip extension and sharing via Dropshare.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is a power user’s kind of utility. The developer is friendly and responsive, and the app fits into your workflow without forcing you to change how you work. It’s particularly well suited to juggling multiple projects at once. There’s also a two-week free trial, which is plenty of time to see whether it fits your workflow.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Real-World Uses&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;After a few weeks of using Dockside, certain workflows start to feel natural.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Temporary file staging&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Drag files from Finder, Mail, or Safari into Dockside while collecting materials for something. Once everything is there, drag them out together into the destination app.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Screenshot triage&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Screenshots land in the secondary shelf automatically. From there you can preview them with Quick Look, drop them into an image tool, or send them directly to a drop zone action.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Automation trigger pad&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Drop a file onto a zone that runs a Shortcut or shell script; resize images, move files to project folders, or trigger upload workflows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Multi-project juggling&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Use separate scratchpad zones for active work, reference material, and future tasks without scattering Finder windows everywhere.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Details&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Activation on up to three Macs&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Apple notarized&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Privacy policy: no data collection; internet used mainly for license activation and checks&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Homebrew install supported (&lt;code&gt;brew install --cask dockside&lt;/code&gt;)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Cost: $5.99 lifetime; no subscription. I could easily see paying five times that for something this useful.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Developer website:&lt;br&gt;&lt;a href="https://hachipoo.com/dockside-app"&gt;Dockside for Mac — native file shelf &amp;amp; Dock companion (drag, drop, done)&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Verdict&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dockside is one of those tools that feels small at first and then quietly becomes part of your daily workflow.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you move files between apps constantly, collect materials for projects, or run file-based automations, it’s an easy recommendation. It behaves like a natural extension of macOS rather than another utility window competing for your attention.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Dockside%20Turns%20Drag-And-Drop%20Into%20a%20Real%20Workflow" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Most Mac users already rely on drag-and-drop constantly, but macOS never really gave us a good place to stage things temporarily. Finder windows work, but they’re clumsy for quick hand-offs between apps.

Dockside turns that gap into a system. It acts like a permanent drop zone beside your Dock where...</summary>

&lt;p&gt;I’m looking for feedback on a few apps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I’m looking for the answers to the following questions:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Did this app solve a problem you had? If so, what was the issue and the solution.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Who do you think is the target audience for the app&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;What’s your favorite feature or biggest aggravation with the app?&lt;/li&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://getbookshelves.app/"&gt;BookShelves eBook Reader -&lt;/a&gt; BookShelves is a modern ebook reader and library manager for macOS and iOS. It supports EPUB, PDF, MOBI, PRC, and Kindle formats with iCloud sync, a customizable reading experience, and thousands of free classic books built in.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://sidebarapp.net/"&gt;Sidebar -&lt;/a&gt; Sidebar is a MacOS application that replaces the standard MacOS Dock. It feels more like the taskbar of other operating systems (e.g. Windows, Linux).&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.vaultsort.com/"&gt;VaultSort - Organize, Secure, and Optimize Your Mac Files -&lt;/a&gt; File automation, cleanup, and security&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://pacificcoast.dev/#procman"&gt;Procman -&lt;/a&gt; Procman is a native process explorer for Mac that combines the hierarchy of pstree with the clarity of Activity Monitor. Instead of a flat list of processes, it shows a live parent-child tree so you can actually understand what spawned what, what’s consuming resources, and how everything fits together.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.liqoria.com/"&gt;Liqoria - Mac Music Player • Apple Music • Spotify • YouTube and more -&lt;/a&gt; An Apple Music alternative, improving your Spotify for Mac workflow, or comparing tools like Cider for Mac.&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>tag:appaddict.app,2005:Post/16115</id>
    <published>2026-04-14T01:06:50Z</published>
    <updated>2026-04-14T01:29:10Z</updated>
    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/learning-and-using-github-as-a-non-developer-with-tower"/>
    <title>Learning and Using GitHub As a Non-Developer with Tower</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" alt="Tower" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzJRQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a1f50152e6731aaff8f371c23c43bdbb8fccfeb3/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFJQUNHa0NBQVk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2Q25OMGNtbHdWRG9NY1hWaGJHbDBlV2xrIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--daf4078a1aefa3c961be2c7b8fbe4a74a2641c0c/CleanShot%202026-04-13%20at%2021.02.32.jpg" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
    &lt;figcaption class="attachment__caption text-center"&gt;
      Tower
    &lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For years I assumed GitHub was only useful if you were a developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Turns out it's actually one of the best tools I've found for managing &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;text-heavy Mac workflows&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I now use Git repositories to version and back up things like:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;my 13K-file Obsidian vault (private)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;~700 Keyboard Maestro macros (public)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Hazel and BetterTouchTool configs (public)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;writing projects and scripts (private)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;~500 Markdown documents with my quotes collection (public)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No coding required.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I recently switched from GitHub Desktop to &lt;a href="https://www.git-tower.com"&gt;Tower&lt;/a&gt;, which exposes a lot more of Git's capabilities without forcing you into the command line.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're a Mac power user managing large folders of Markdown, scripts, or automation configs, Git is basically &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Time Machine for specific folders&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; — and Tower makes it easy to use.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why This Matters for Mac Power Users&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you work with text-heavy workflows on macOS — Markdown notes, scripts, automation configs, or documentation — Git gives you something Time Machine doesn’t:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• version history for individual files&lt;br&gt;• the ability to roll back one specific edit&lt;br&gt;• an off-site backup of critical working folders&lt;br&gt;• synchronization between multiple Macs&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For people managing large Obsidian vaults, automation libraries, or documentation projects, that combination becomes extremely useful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Let's Speak the Same Language&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here's a quick translation of common Git terminology:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Repository&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A folder tracked by Git that contains files and their complete change history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Commit&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A saved snapshot of the repository at a specific moment, along with a message describing the change.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;History&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The chronological record of all commits.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Branch&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A parallel line of development that lets you experiment without affecting the main version.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Merge&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Combining changes from one branch into another.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Remote&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A copy of the repository stored somewhere else; typically GitHub.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Push&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Send your local commits to the remote repository.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Pull&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Fetch changes from the remote repository and integrate them into your local copy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Clone&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Download a complete copy of a repository, including its history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Diff&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A comparison showing exactly what changed between two versions of a file.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Why I Use Tower&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower provides a graphical interface for Git repositories and remote services such as GitHub. Instead of memorizing commands, you interact with commits, branches, and history visually.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For developers this manages source code. For everyone else it manages &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;collections of important files&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Git tracks the complete history of a folder. Every time you make a commit, Git records a snapshot of the repository. Tower simply exposes that system visually. Instead of typing commands like:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;pre data-language="plain"&gt;git add &lt;br&gt;git commit &lt;br&gt;git push&lt;/pre&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower gives you:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• checkboxes to stage files&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• a commit message box&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• push / pull buttons&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;• a visual timeline of changes&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The idea is so simple it's easy to miss how powerful it is.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Every commit becomes a permanent historical snapshot.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For writers, note-takers, and automation nerds, Git effectively becomes &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Time Machine for specific folders&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;; but with far more precision. Instead of restoring an entire folder, you can restore a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;single edit inside a single file&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. That capability becomes extremely valuable once your knowledge base grows large.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;I regularly use Tower to manage:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Markdown notes&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;scripts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;documentation&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;configuration files&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;knowledge bases&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;writing projects

&lt;br&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Using Tower with GitHub adds a few major benefits:&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;
&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;complete version history&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;off-site backup&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;synchronization between machines&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;detailed change tracking&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Tower Features Worth Highlighting&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Rebase&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower includes a visual interface for &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;rebasing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, which allows you to reorganize commit history. The GUI makes operations that are intimidating on the command line much easier:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;reordering commits&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;editing commit messages&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;combining commits&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Stashing&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose you're halfway through editing files but need to switch branches. You don't want to commit unfinished work. &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Stashing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt; temporarily saves those changes so you can switch contexts and return later.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Conflict Resolution&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I'll admit I tend to use more computers than I should. That occasionally creates conflicts. When multiple versions of a file diverge, Git produces a &lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;merge conflict&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;. Tower provides a visual interface for resolving these conflicts instead of forcing you to edit raw conflict markers. For non-developers, this feature alone removes a lot of confusion.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Getting Started in Five Minutes&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can realistically start using Tower on macOS in about five minutes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Create a repository&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Pick a folder; your Obsidian vault is a good candidate. Initialize it as a Git repository in Tower.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;**Make the first commit&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tower will show all files in the folder. Select them and create the first commit.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Connect to GitHub&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Create a repository on GitHub and link it to your local repository. Push the files.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Adopt a simple daily workflow&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Open Tower; review the files that changed; write a short commit message; push to GitHub.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's really all most non-developers need.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Details&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Tower Website&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.git-tower.com"&gt;https://www.git-tower.com&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Privacy Policy&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.git-tower.com/legal/privacy-policy"&gt;https://www.git-tower.com/legal/privacy-policy&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Price&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;$5.75/month billed annually&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Learning%20and%20Using%20GitHub%20As%20a%20Non-Developer%20with%20Tower" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

Turns out it's actually one of the best tools I've found for managing text-heavy Mac workflows.

I now use Git repositories to version and back up things like:

• my 13K-file Obsidian vault (private)
